objectives: Explain why Modbus TCP traffic can be read by anyone on the network path
Capture plant traffic and narrow it down with Wireshark display filters
Decode register values that carry text into characters
Describe why sniffing is hard to detect and which defences limit it
takeaways: Modbus TCP is plaintext: function codes, addresses and values are readable in every captured packet.
A switch only forwards traffic to its destination, so sniffing needs a position on the path.
Display filters such as modbus.func_code turn thousands of packets into the few that matter.
Each 16-bit register can hold two characters, so text can hide in process data.
Passive sniffing sends nothing, so defenders protect capture positions, segment and encrypt instead of waiting for an alert.

checkpoints.question: You want to see only requests that write several registers at once. Which display filter fits?
options: modbus.func_code == 6
modbus.func_code == 16
modbus.func_code == 15
checkpoints.explanation: Function code 16 is Write Multiple Registers. Code 6 also writes a register, but only one per request, and code 15 writes several values at once, but to coils rather than registers. Telling these three apart is the key to filtering a Modbus capture.

quiz.question: Why can a captured Modbus TCP packet be read directly?
options: Wireshark breaks the weak Modbus encryption
Modbus TCP is not encrypted at all
Modbus sends its fields as readable text, like HTTP
The PLC sends a copy of each packet to every host
quiz.explanation: Modbus TCP has neither encryption nor authentication, so nothing is being broken. It is tempting to think plaintext means text, but Modbus is a binary format; it is public, so Wireshark can decode every field.

quiz.question: You start Wireshark on a laptop plugged into a normal switch port of the plant network. Why might you see almost none of the PLC's traffic?
options: The PLC encrypts traffic to unknown laptops
A switch only delivers packets to their destination
Wireshark cannot decode Modbus without a plugin
Your laptop needs an IP address in the PLC's subnet first
quiz.explanation: Switches learn where each device is and deliver traffic only there, so other conversations never reach your port. An IP address does not change that, because a capture is passive and only sees what arrives. To see others' traffic you need a mirror port, a tap, the host of a virtual network, or a man-in-the-middle position.

quiz.question: A register holds the value 18533, which is 0x4865 in hexadecimal. Read as two ASCII characters, what is it?
options: "eH"
"He"
"HE"
quiz.explanation: Modbus sends the high byte first. 0x48 is 'H' and 0x65 is a lower-case 'e', so the register reads "He". Swapping the bytes into "eH" is the most common mistake; an upper-case 'E' would be 0x45.

quiz.question: Why does the CybICS IDS not alert when you sniff the plant traffic?
options: The IDS is paused while a capture is running
A passive capture sends no packets to see
The IDS ignores traffic from the landing page
Wireshark hides its packets from the IDS
quiz.explanation: Detection systems look for traffic, and a passive capture adds none; there is nothing for Wireshark to hide. The steps around it, such as ARP spoofing to get onto the path, can be detected, which is why defenders watch for those.

quiz.question: Which measures reduce what an attacker can learn by sniffing? (Select all that apply)
options: Protecting switch mirror ports and network taps
Encrypting traffic between zones, for example with a VPN or Modbus/TCP Security
Keeping secrets out of registers
Moving Modbus from port 502 to another port
quiz.explanation: Fewer capture positions, encrypted links and no secrets in process data all limit what a capture reveals. Moving Modbus to another port changes nothing in the bytes: they are still plaintext, and Wireshark can be told to decode them as Modbus on any port.
